newsitem.title: DJIBOUTI: Djibouti seeks $87 million in aid for recovery.
newsitem.headline: Djibouti seeks $87 million in aid for recovery.

text.p: The government of Djibouti, one of the world's poorest countries, is to ask donors in Geneva on Thursday for $87 million in aid to revive the largely barren nation at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The money would be used to rebuild the economy, pay bonuses to demobilised troops and reduce the impact of the demobilisation programme on the budget.
The proposal said Djibouti planned to cut the armed forces by 8,452 from a current 18,000 over 18 months. The government has demobilised 4,000 soldiers since late 1993.

Civil war between 1991 and 1994 doubled military spending in Djibouti. More than 40 per cent of its gross domestic product comes from the French community of some 8,500 including 3,500 military personnel.
Djibouti's total internal and external debt is twice annual government spending.
The government said it planned to resettle 18,000 people of the Afar tribe who fled war zones in southwest and north Djibouti in the civil war. Half took refuge in Djibouti city.
The programme promises the private sector a prominent role in putting the tiny country's economy back on track, officials said.
The recovery plan also urged donors to write off 20 percent or $17.5 million of external debt of the Djibouti port and airport authorities.
It said the treasury, customs and tax authorities would be modernised using computers with French and European Union aid.
The government has borrowed $87 million from the five largest state-owned companies and as part of reforms has agreed to involve private investors gradually in running state firms.
The government pledged to look into how to remove "useless positions" from the bloated civil service of 7,000 employees.
Djibouti is under a structural adjustment programme of the International Monetary Fund which is due to end in May and aimed to revive the economy to two percent growth by the year 2000.
But Djibouti's per capita income shrank by 20 percent from 1990 to 1994.
